Practicing meditation can help you to recognize the troublesome thoughts and emotions and deal with them constructively but it comes from a less analytical perspective than CBT techniques. Both methods eventually have you recognizing an unhelpful thought or emotion.

Meditation isn't blanking one's mind but more of an exercise in focus on one's senses. Distracting thoughts are normal and to be expected but the secret or goal of mindful meditation is to recognize/acknowledge the thought or emotion and then let it go, returning to focus on your senses. Most practices have you focus on your breath as you belly breathe while sitting (could be in a chair) with good posture. In yoga you also focus on the breath but also other sensations, like the pressure of your weight against the ground.

It takes time, and can be discouraging when you realize you have been thinking of something else for most of the session, but with regular practice (start trying to make 2 minutes per day) the focus becomes easier and there are fewer distracting thoughts. Yoga may be a more accessible form of mindful meditation but it comes with its own distractions (other people in the class, having to listen for instruction, wondering if you've got the posture right....)

It is also important to not get frustrated with yourself for the constant distracting thoughts. They are normal. Most of us live always reacting to our thoughts and emotions and rarely do we see how they affect our thinking.

Our emotions are a system of the body that tells you something. 'Being Sad' is similar to 'seeing white'--it's something that happens because of your body state. A Long Tail phenomenon (as predicted by Alvin Toffler) now characterizes contemporary culture, leading to an apparent increasing incoherence of activism. Traditional activism has been conducted largely in the urban setting, focused on urban centers of political and economic power and concentrations of the wealthy and relying on a concentration of certain class segments in cities to facilitate physical activity. But the urban habitat has been militarized, the poor moved to an outer-urban perimeter and more confined communities, the middle-class to distant suburbs (not that they were all that activism-inclined anyway), and the rich to isolated enclaves and the edge of wilderness. Corporations also no longer concentrate in cities, now often set in suburban 'campuses' where they can impose much greater security and physical separation and anonymity from the people they impact. Americans have the least amount of vacation time in the developed world, and this likewise impedes their ability to organize and engage in activism. It is logistically much more difficult today to engage in activism than it was in the past, and so it's been relegated to young people with more freedom of movement. The internet has facilitated new means for people to communicate and organize, but, again, that's largely limited to the young with greater computer literacy, and overcoming the physical/geographical barriers to organizing activity remains difficult. The potential power of the 'virtual community' was greatly over-estimated as it lacked mechanisms for building trust and physically expressing itself in significant ways. Mass protests often seem more common in Europe than the US, possibly because there is that much greater an urban population, a broader urban demographic, and people with more free time on their hands.

So vital activism today is less about fighting or speaking truth to power and more about simply routing around it. And this we see expressed in things like Bitcoin which is, quite simply, an attempt to route around the power, obstructions, and toll booths of traditional financial systems. Similarly we see the Maker movement, which has as a key undercurrent the meme of 'unplugging'; the leveraging of technologies of personal/independent production of the paring-away of market dependencies. And in a broader context we have the Open Source, P2P, and new Commons movements which are about leveraging emerging technology's potential for zero marginal costs and the organization of social capital on the disruption of Industrial Age economics and its hegemonies and power structures.
